title.text:
Text as data and
meaning as numbers

objects.text: How can a computer compare customer messages when it only understands numbers?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 21 of 24  |  Module E: Neural networks and text
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Until now every variable we used held numbers or short labels. Today a variable holds a sentence. We take eight hundred customer messages from Lakeside Mart and turn them into numbers in two ways. First by counting words, then with embeddings, which put meaning into numbers.

You will build a sentiment classifier, and a search that can find a long queue complaint written in different words.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can clean customer messages and turn them into numbers, first with a bag of words and TF-IDF, and then train a sentiment classifier on them. You can score a search against an answer key, and you can explain why counting words fails on a message such as not good.

And you can turn messages into embeddings and rank them by cosine similarity, which is how a semantic search works. All of it runs on the eight hundred Lakeside Mart feedback messages.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts first, then
a Python lab on customer messages

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Pictures and plain words first. Then you open the notebook. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
Two hours again. We start with ten minutes of recall and today's question. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with laptops closed, so you can follow the pictures. After the break you open a Colab notebook for forty-five minutes. You will clean the messages, count words, train a sentiment classifier, score a keyword search against an answer key, and then try a search by meaning.

The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. Please protect the lab time, because that is where the ideas stick.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What does one artificial neuron compute?
2.  What does training a neural network do?
3.  When do you keep a simpler model instead of a neural network?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 20. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What does one artificial neuron compute?

A good answer is this. A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function such as sigmoid or ReLU.

Question two. What does training a neural network do?

A good answer is this. It repeats small corrections, by gradient descent with backpropagation, to lower the loss function.

Question three. When do you keep a simpler model instead of a neural network?

A good answer is this. When the simpler model scores about the same on the test set. It is cheaper and easier to explain (parsimony).

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 20

rows.text: What does one artificial neuron compute?
A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function such as sigmoid or ReLU.
What does training a neural network do?
It repeats small corrections, by gradient descent with backpropagation, to lower the loss function.
When do you keep a simpler model instead of a neural network?
When the simpler model scores about the same on the test set. It is cheaper and easier to explain (parsimony).

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_gear_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.50.png

slides.notes:
Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. One artificial neuron multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the total through an activation function. Training repeats small corrections, using gradient descent and backpropagation, to make the loss function smaller. And you keep the simpler model when its test score is about the same, which is called parsimony.

That last idea matters today, because the simplest text model we build will do very well. Which answer did you find hardest?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Cleaning raw text into tokens: lowercase it, remove noise with a regular expression, split it into words and drop filler words.
Bag of words counts each word in each message and ignores the order. TF-IDF weights those counts so rare words count more.
A supervised model that gives each message a label, such as positive, neutral or negative.
A list of numbers that stands for the meaning of a message. Messages with similar meanings get similar vectors.
A score from -1 to 1 for how alike two vectors are. Semantic search ranks messages by that score.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Text preprocessing (tokenisation, stop words). Cleaning raw text into tokens: lowercase it, remove noise with a regular expression, split it into words and drop filler words.

Bag of words and TF-IDF. Bag of words counts each word in each message and ignores the order. TF-IDF weights those counts so rare words count more.

Text classification (sentiment analysis). A supervised model that gives each message a label, such as positive, neutral or negative.

Embedding (vector). A list of numbers that stands for the meaning of a message. Messages with similar meanings get similar vectors.

Cosine similarity and semantic search. A score from -1 to 1 for how alike two vectors are. Semantic search ranks messages by that score.

title.text:
Text is unstructured data: a sentence
has no fixed columns to count

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_msgtable_7.70x4.80_28f8d832.png
objects.alt: Text is unstructured data: a sentence has no fixed columns to count

objects.text: Unstructured data has no fixed columns. Free text is the most common kind.

runs.text: feedback.csv holds 800 customer messages. Variable type: text (string).
A model needs a vector: an ordered list of numbers.
So we turn each message into a vector.

slides.notes:
Until now every variable was a number or a short label. Look at feedback dot csv. It has 800 customer messages, and the message variable is free text. That is unstructured data, which means there are no fixed columns inside a sentence for you to count or add up.

The other variables are neat. Rating is a number, sentiment is a mood label, and theme says what the message is about. A model can only use numbers, so today is about one job: turning each message into a vector, an ordered list of numbers. How would you turn a sentence into numbers in Excel?

title.text:
Every text method follows the same path:
clean, make vectors, then classify or search

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_65b34fb0.png
objects.alt: Every text method follows the same path: clean, make vectors, then classify or search

objects.text: Today we walk this path twice: with counted words, and with embeddings.

slides.notes:
This is the map for the whole session. Raw text goes in on the left. Text preprocessing cleans it. Then we make vectors, either by counting words or by using an embedding. A model or a search uses the vectors, a classifier to give a label or a similarity score to find messages.

And the last box, evaluation, checks the result against an answer key. Every text project at work follows this path, whatever the tools are. We walk it twice today. Which box do you think takes the most time in real projects?

title.text:
Text preprocessing changes one real message in four
steps: lowercase, regex, tokenise, drop stop words

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_preprocess_11.90x4.25_e9f4f143.png
objects.alt: Text preprocessing changes one real message in four steps: lowercase, regex, tokenise, drop stop words

objects.text: Message F0001 of feedback.csv. Each step feeds the next.

slides.notes:
Here is text preprocessing on one real message, F0001. The original has a label at the start and a polite phrase at the end. Step one, lowercasing, so that Fresh and fresh count as the same word. Step two, regex cleaning: a regular expression removes the opener, the closer and the punctuation.

Step three, tokenisation, splits the text into tokens, which here are words. Step four removes stop words, filler words such as for. The result is four tokens. In Excel you did this with LOWER, SUBSTITUTE and TRIM. Which step changed the message most?

title.text:
A regular expression (regex) is a pattern that
finds text, and one line cleans 800 messages

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_regex_7.70x4.80_0542242d.png
objects.alt: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern that finds text, and one line cleans 800 messages

objects.text: A regex is Find and Replace with wildcards. Python applies it with re.sub or str.replace.

runs.text: Messages here open with Hello. or Feedback: and close with Please reply.
After we strip those lines, \bnot\b matches 35 messages, down from 88.
Test a regex on a few rows first.

slides.notes:
A regular expression, or regex, is a pattern that describes text to find or replace. You can think of it as Find and Replace with wildcards. Look at the four patterns. The first matches any character that is not a letter or a space, so it removes punctuation.

The second matches the whole word not. In the raw file it matches 88 messages, but many of those are the polite closing line I am not happy, added to the end. After we strip the opener and closer lines, it matches 35. The lesson is to test a regex on a few real rows before you apply it to all of them.

Why might a closing line mislead a model?

title.text:
The most common words are filler, and stop word
removal exposes the words that carry meaning

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_topwords_11.90x4.25_ae1c4e11.png
objects.alt: The most common words are filler, and stop word removal exposes the words that carry meaning

objects.text: Messages containing each word, out of 800. Keep the word not: many stop word lists remove it.

slides.notes:
The left chart counts, for each word, how many of the 800 raw messages contain it. The winners are the, at, I, please and on, which say nothing about mood or topic. Stop words are such filler words, and removing them is the fourth preprocessing step. The right chart shows the words that remain after cleaning, where phone, please and Kampala lead.

Please stays in because it is not on our stop list. In a real project you decide whether polite words belong on your own list. Look at the caption. Many standard stop word lists contain the word not. If you delete it, you delete the signal that flips a meaning.

So read your list before you use it. Which word on the right surprised you?

title.text:
A bag of words counts each word in
each message and ignores the order

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_dtm_11.90x4.25_8481c2f1.png
objects.alt: A bag of words counts each word in each message and ignores the order

objects.text: A document-term matrix (count vectorizer). The full file is 800 messages by 267 words.

slides.notes:
This is a bag of words. Take three real messages, A, B and C, all from Jinja. Each row of the table is one message, and each column is one word from the vocabulary, which is the list of all different words. The cell holds how many times the word appears.

Message A contains not twice, so its not cell is 2. The order of the words is thrown away, which is why we call it a bag. This table is called a document-term matrix. For all 800 messages after cleaning it has 267 columns, one per different word.

Most cells are zero. Which word do messages B and C share?

title.text:
TF-IDF multiplies a word count by how
rare the word is across all messages

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.95_7edad8f7.png
objects.alt: TF-IDF multiplies a word count by how rare the word is across all messages

rows.text: Term frequency: times word t appears in message d
Document frequency: messages that contain word t
Natural logarithm. A rarer word gives a larger value

objects.text: scikit-learn adds 1 inside the logarithm and 1 outside, so its numbers differ from ours.

slides.notes:
TF-IDF stands for term frequency, inverse document frequency. The term frequency is the count of a word in one message. The document frequency is the number of messages that contain the word at all. The inverse document frequency is the natural logarithm of N divided by that document frequency.

Our worked number: the word queue is in 19 of 800 messages, so ln of 800 over 19 is 3.74. In this textbook formula a word in every message gets zero. Multiply the count by the weight and rare words count more. scikit-learn adds one inside the logarithm and one outside, so there a word in every message gets one, and its values differ from ours.

What would idf be for a word in every message here?

title.text:
Rare words get more weight: idf
is 0.52 for the and 4.74 for costly

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_17a9132b.png
objects.alt: Rare words get more weight: idf is 0.52 for the and 4.74 for costly

objects.text: Inverse document frequency (idf) shrinks words found in many messages and raises words found in few.

runs.text: Computed on all 800 raw messages, before stop words are removed.
TF-IDF down-weights filler even when you keep it.
Then each message vector is scaled to length 1.

slides.notes:
Here is idf for five real words, computed on the raw messages before any stop words are removed. The appears in 476 messages, so its idf is only 0.52. At gets 0.80 and please gets 1.21. The word queue appears in 19 messages and gets 3.74. The word costly appears in 7 messages and gets 4.74.

So filler is shrunk automatically, and rare words stand out. After weighting, we scale each message vector to length one so long messages do not win just by being long. Why might a very rare word be a poor feature?

title.text:
A sentiment classifier learns one
weight per word for each label

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_word_weights_7.70x4.80_1385471d.png
objects.alt: A sentiment classifier learns one weight per word for each label

objects.text: Text classification: a supervised model learns from messages with known labels.

runs.text: Features: the TF-IDF value of each word.
The chart shows the five largest learned weights for each label.

slides.notes:
Sentiment analysis is a classification problem, and it is called text classification when the input is text. The target is the sentiment label. The features are the TF-IDF values of the words. The model here is multinomial logistic regression, which you can think of as logistic regression with one set of weights per label.

We use a small numpy version so every number is checkable. In practice you would use LogisticRegression. Look at the chart, which comes from a model fitted on all 800 messages. For the positive label the biggest weights go to good, quick and quickly. For negative, not, shouted and than.

For neutral, available, bought and tell, the words of questions. Does that match your common sense?

title.text:
A random split flatters the score: 565 of 800
test messages repeat a training message

objects.text: Shuffled 5-fold: 94.2%

runs.text: 565 of 800 test messages repeat a training text.
Data leakage: the score is too high.

objects.text: Grouped 5-fold: 77.4%

runs.text: Copies of one text share a fold.

objects.text: Use the grouped score. The baseline is 50.6%.

slides.notes:
This file has 800 messages, but only 360 different texts after cleaning, because the generator repeats sentences with different openers and closers. If we shuffle the messages and cut them into five folds, copies of one text land in both the training and the test side. In my run, 565 of the 800 test messages had a twin in the training data, and the score came out at 94.2%.

That is data leakage, which you met in Session 16. The fix is grouped cross-validation: all copies of one text go to the same fold. The score drops to 77.4%, which is the honest one. The baseline, always saying negative, is 50.6%. Why would real customer messages also need a grouped split?

title.text:
Grouped cross-validation gives 77.4%
accuracy against 50.6% for the baseline

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_confusion3_7.70x4.80_de80f595.png
objects.alt: Grouped cross-validation gives 77.4% accuracy against 50.6% for the baseline

objects.text: 619 of 800 messages are right when the model has never seen their text.

runs.text: Five folds of 160 messages, each predicted by a model trained on the other four.

slides.notes:
We cut the 800 messages into five folds. Each fold was predicted by a model trained on the other four, and no text appears on both sides. This is the confusion matrix of all 800 predictions. Rows are the true label, columns are what the model said, and the gold diagonal holds the correct answers.

The model is right on 619 messages, which is 77.4%. The majority-class baseline, which says negative every time, scores 50.6%, so the model clearly beats it. Look at the fold scores: they run from 63.7% to 86.2%. A single split would have given one of those, which is why we report the average.

About six percent of the labels are wrong on purpose, so a perfect score is out of reach. Where are the 181 wrong answers on the matrix?

title.text:
Read the mistakes before you trust the score:
some are bad labels and some are model errors

rows.text: Mobile money payment went through quickly, thank you.
Model wrong: the message is positive, and its words never appeared in the other folds.
Delivery was on time and the groceries were cold. Thank you.
Feedback: I was charged twice for one purchase. Thank you.
Label looks wrong: the message is a complaint.
Staff were rude when I asked about a refund for bread.
Label looks wrong: the message is a complaint.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.50.png

objects.text: 4 of the 181 mistakes. Real messages vary more than these 360 texts, so expect lower scores at work.

slides.notes:
Never stop at the score. Read the mistakes. Here are four of the 181 wrong answers. In the first row the model is wrong about a clearly positive message, because its words never appeared in the training folds. The second is mixed, so a person could argue either way.

In the last two rows the label looks wrong: a complaint labelled positive and a complaint labelled neutral. That is part of the six percent of noisy labels. There is a warning in the note. The file was generated from only 360 different texts. Real customer messages vary far more, and an accuracy like this would fall.

Which row would you fix first?

title.text:
Counting words cannot read negation:
our model still calls "not good" positive

objects.text: The queue was good
The queue was not good

runs.text: Wrong: the word good still outweighs the word not.

objects.text: A bag of words sees words and ignores their order. Models that read word order do better.

slides.notes:
This is the classic failure of counting words. I typed two new sentences and ran our trained classifier on both. For the queue was good it says positive, with probability 0.94. Fine. For the queue was not good it still says positive, with probability 0.72. The model gives some negative weight to the word not, but the positive weight of good is bigger.

Another model or another setting may get this one sentence right, but a bag of words cannot read negation by design. It only learns that the word not often appears in negative messages. What other short words flip a meaning?

title.text:
In practice you use the scikit-learn recipe:
TfidfVectorizer, LogisticRegression and a pipeline

objects.text:
Expected accuracy: about 0.79
(folds 0.71 to 0.88; numpy replica)
In plain words

runs.text: CountVectorizer builds the bag of words. TfidfVectorizer builds TF-IDF.
make_pipeline chains the vectoriser and the classifier, so the vocabulary and idf come from the training folds only.
GroupKFold keeps copies of one text together.
scikit-learn idf for queue is 4.69, not 3.74, because of its smoothing.

slides.notes:
This is how a team does it with real tools. A TfidfVectorizer turns the cleaned texts into TF-IDF vectors. Its sibling, CountVectorizer, gives plain counts, which is the bag of words. LogisticRegression is the classifier. make_pipeline chains the two, so that during cross-validation the vocabulary and the idf values are learned from the training folds only.

That avoids a second kind of leak. GroupKFold keeps copies of one text together. Our numpy copy of this recipe gives about 0.79, and your Colab run may differ by a point or two. The scikit-learn formula adds one inside the logarithm and one outside, so queue gets 4.69 there.

Why does the pipeline matter for honest scores?

title.text:
A keyword search for queue finds
only 28% of the queue messages

objects.text: We search the 360 different texts, so copies cannot inflate the result. The word queue is in 10 of the 36 texts whose theme is queue (recall). All 10 hits are right (precision 100 percent).

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_ff92e05a.png
objects.alt: A keyword search for queue finds only 28% of the queue messages

slides.notes:
Now we use the theme variable as an answer key. The theme says what a message is about. We search the 360 different texts, one row per text, so that ten copies of one sentence cannot fill the results. 36 of those texts are about queues. A keyword search for the word queue finds 10 texts, and all of them are about queues.

That is a precision of one hundred percent: every result is right. But recall is 28%: it finds only 10 of the 36. The other texts say line, wait, slow or too many people. High precision with low recall is the typical weakness of a keyword search. Which would your manager care about more, a missed complaint or a wrong one?

title.text:
Adding keywords raises recall but lowers
precision, and you must guess every synonym

rows.text: Twelve words: queue, line, wait, slow, till, checkout ...

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.50.png

objects.text: Precision = right hits divided by hits found. Recall = right hits divided by all 36 queue texts. A search for "crowded cashier" returns 6 of 10 texts about staff and only 4 about queues.

slides.notes:
Here is the trade-off, on the 360 different texts. Searching for queue alone finds 10 texts, all right. Adding the word line raises recall to 53%. Adding wait and waited finds more but lets in 1 wrong one. With twelve words we reach recall of one hundred percent, but precision drops to 75%, because words such as pay and counter appear in other kinds of text.

And you needed the answer key to know which words to add. A query with different words does worse: searching for crowded cashier puts 6 texts about staff in the top ten. Hence the idea of searching by meaning. How would you know which synonyms to add?

title.text:
An embedding is a vector of numbers placed
so that similar meanings sit close together

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_embed_map_7.70x4.80_62193ccc.png
objects.alt: An embedding is a vector of numbers placed so that similar meanings sit close together

objects.text: An embedding turns a message into a vector. Messages with similar meaning get nearby vectors.

runs.text: Illustrative: the positions are made up.
A real embedding has hundreds of numbers: 384 for all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (model card).
You compute real ones in Colab.

slides.notes:
Now the second way to turn text into numbers. An embedding is a vector, a list of numbers, produced by a model that was trained on a very large amount of text. The training makes messages with similar meaning land near each other. This picture is illustrative: I made up the positions and used only two axes so you can see the idea.

Three messages about waiting sit together, two about fresh food sit together, and two about prices sit together. Real embeddings have hundreds of numbers instead of two. The sentence-transformers model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 gives 384, according to its model card. Which two messages on the picture are closest?

title.text:
Cosine similarity measures the angle between
two vectors, so length does not matter

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_k_cosine_7.70x4.80_6e0452c0.png
objects.alt: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, so length does not matter

objects.text: Cosine similarity runs from -1 to 1. Close to 1 means a very similar direction.

runs.text: 1 means the same direction: very similar.
0 means a right angle: nothing in common.

slides.notes:
Cosine similarity is the standard score for how alike two vectors are. Think of each vector as an arrow from the origin. Cosine looks only at the angle between two arrows, so a long message and a short message about the same thing still match. These three pairs are illustrative vectors with two numbers each, and I calculated the cosines in numpy.

The two arrows on the left point almost the same way, so the cosine is nearly one. In the middle they point in different directions, about 0.47. On the right they point in opposite directions, minus one. Which pair would you call similar meaning?

title.text:
Cosine similarity is the dot product
divided by the two vector lengths

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x2.33_48660062.png
objects.alt: Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the two vector lengths

rows.text: Dot product: multiply matching numbers, then add
Length of vector a: the square root of the sum of squares
Two queue messages that differ only in the town
A queue message and "No queue at all", then a mobile money message

slides.notes:
Here is the formula. The top is the dot product: multiply the matching numbers of the two vectors and add them. The bottom is the product of the two lengths, where a length is the square root of the sum of squares. Our illustrative vectors are three four and four three.

The dot product is 24, both lengths are five, so the cosine is twenty four over twenty five, which is 0.96. The bottom rows use real TF-IDF vectors. Two long queue messages that differ only in the town score 0.92. A queue message and the message No queue at all score 0.24, and a mobile money message scores 0.00, because they share no word.

Why is the last one exactly zero?

title.text:
Semantic search ranks messages by the cosine
similarity of their embeddings to the query

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_2e6e3aa8.png
objects.alt: Semantic search ranks messages by the cosine similarity of their embeddings to the query

objects.text: The recipe is identical for TF-IDF vectors. Only the vectors change.

slides.notes:
This is semantic search, step by step. First, embed every different text once and keep the vectors. Second, embed the search query with the same model. Third, compute the cosine similarity between the query vector and every message vector. Fourth, rank the messages by that score and keep the top k, for example the top ten.

Fifth, evaluate: count how many of the top ten really have the theme queue. That count divided by ten is precision at k, and we use it again next session. The recipe is the same for TF-IDF vectors. Only the vectors change. Why do we embed the messages only once?

title.text:
Messages can hold personal data: remove
it with a regex before you analyse

objects.text: Before (illustrative)

runs.text: Call me on 0700 000 111 about my refund.
A phone number is personal data.

objects.text: After the regex

runs.text: Call me on PHONE_REMOVED about my refund.
Names in free text are personal data too.

objects.text: My understanding: the Uganda Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 covers personal data. Ask your data officer. Not legal advice.

slides.notes:
Customers sometimes type personal details into a message, such as a phone number. That is personal data, and the person is the data subject. My understanding is that the Uganda Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2019 covers it, and the organisation that decides how the data is used is the data controller.

I am not giving legal advice, so ask your data officer. A practical step is to remove such details with a regex before the text goes into any analysis or tool. The example on the slide is made up. Do your own work messages ever contain phone numbers?
